name: Hair henna (cosmetic henna)

card.summary: A powdered plant dye from Lawsonia inermis leaves that stains hair orange to auburn to burgundy, used to colour grey hair or add red tones without synthetic dye.
card.aka: Lawsonia inermis, mehndi, natural red hair dye, henna rinse
card.note: Products sold as 'black henna' may contain PPD, which can cause severe allergic reactions; rare pigmentation reactions to pure henna are also reported.

quick.overview:
Hair henna is a powder made from the dried, ground leaves of the henna shrub. Its dye molecule, lawsone, binds to hair keratin and gives a permanent-feeling stain in orange, auburn or burgundy tones. People use it to cover grey, deepen red tones or tint hair without ammonia-based dye, and it is combined with indigo for brown and black shades.

Henna has been used on hair since ancient Egypt and was fashionable in Victorian Europe. Research on it is mostly safety-focused: lawsone absorption through skin, genotoxicity assays, and case reports of allergic or pigmentary reactions, especially to adulterated 'black henna' products.
quick.how: Henna powder is mixed into a paste with a mildly acidic or plain liquid, left to release the dye, applied to the hair and scalp, and left on for a period before rinsing. Colour depends on starting hair colour and the quality of the henna. Cassia (also called neutral henna) is mixed in for lighter reds or golds, and indigo for browns and blacks. Some products sold as 'henna' contain other plant dyes, metal salts or additives, which affects results.
quick.risks: Pure henna is generally regarded as lower risk than synthetic dyes, but case reports describe allergic contact dermatitis and persistent grey-brown facial pigmentation after use. 'Black henna' products can contain para-phenylenediamine (PPD), a potent allergen; sensitisation can be lifelong and can affect later hair-dye use. Henna is listed as hazardous for people with G6PD deficiency. In the EU, a scientific committee in 2002 judged lawsone mutagenic and unsuitable as a hair colorant, while the US FDA permits it as a hair dye with limitations.

lead: Cosmetic henna is a plant-based hair colourant made from the powdered leaves of Lawsonia inermis. The principal colouring compound is lawsone (2-hydroxy-1,4-naphthoquinone), which stains hair a range of reds [3][10]. Users apply it to add warm red, copper or auburn colour, to cover grey, or to colour hair without ammonia, peroxide or PPD-based dyes.

The colour depends on the person's natural shade and on the henna quality: results run from orange through auburn to burgundy. Blending with cassia gives lighter reds or golds and blending with indigo gives browns to black [10]. Henna has a long history in hair care, from ancient Egyptian use to Victorian popularity and a mid-twentieth-century revival [10].

Research on henna as a hair dye mostly concerns safety: skin absorption of lawsone, genotoxicity tests, and clinical reports of allergic and pigmentary reactions, especially to products adulterated with PPD [3][3][4][5].

Covers grey or changes hair colour
angle.text: Henna directly changes hair colour: lawsone binds to the hair shaft, producing orange to burgundy tones, and combining it with indigo or cassia moves the result toward brown, black or golden shades. People use it for grey coverage and for a plant-based alternative to chemical dye.

paras: Henna powder is produced by drying, milling and sifting henna leaves. Mixed with liquid and allowed to rest, the powder releases lawsone, which stains keratin [10]. Hair application uses the paste in a single treatment or repeated treatments, with the colour deepening as layers build up.

Colour results vary. Henna on dark hair adds reddish highlights, while on light or grey hair it shows orange-to-red. Cassia obovata (senna) is used to lighten or tone the result, and indigo is added to move from red to brown and black [10]. 'Neutral henna' is generally cassia powder and does not change hair colour [10]. Some products labelled henna contain other natural dyes, metal salts, oils, waxes or allergens [10].

The hair of the 17th-dynasty Egyptian royal Ahmose-Henuttamehu, dated to about 1574 BCE, was probably dyed with henna [10]. In the nineteenth century, Pre-Raphaelite artists and their circle popularised henna-red hair in Europe, and the singer Adelina Patti is credited with spreading its use [10]. Turkey was a major henna exporter for hair use in the Victorian era, and Lucille Ball's 'henna rinse' on I Love Lucy in the 1950s was followed by popularity among young people in the 1960s [10].

Lawsone absorption through human skin has been studied because the EU scientific committee concluded in 2002 that it was mutagenic and unsuitable as a hair colorant, while the US FDA approves henna with limitations for hair colouring [3]. A genotoxicity assessment of lawsone reviewed earlier findings of weak bacterial mutagenicity in some strains [4].

Clinical reports describe pigmented contact dermatitis, with grey-brown facial pigmentation, after pure henna hair dye use, including cases reported in Korea and a patient whose facial hyperpigmentation followed seven months of monthly henna use [6][8][2]. A Korean multicentre study of 1,033 patients found hair dyes associated with pigmented contact dermatitis, though it concerned hair dyes broadly [1].

Adulterated 'black henna' is a distinct concern. Temporary-tattoo and hair products that mix henna with PPD have caused allergic reactions, and a Budapest patch-test series found PPD sensitivity in 5.75 percent of patients tested [5][7]. A case report describes severe scalp swelling and upper airway compromise after black henna hair dye [9]. PPD sensitisation is lifelong and can lead to reactions to later chemical dyes [10]. Henna is also noted as dangerous for people with G6PD deficiency [10].

No controlled trials of hair henna's cosmetic colour results were found. Published human data consist of an in vitro skin absorption study of lawsone [3], a genotoxicity assessment [4], a large retrospective Korean study of hair dyes and pigmented contact dermatitis [1], PPD patch-test series [7], and case reports of reactions to pure and 'black' henna [2][6][8][9].
